newsitem.title: USA: Coke results bode well for growth - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Coke results bode well for growth - analysts.

text.p: Coca-Cola Co has set the stage for vigorous long-term growth in its global beverage business by strengthening bottling networks overseas and leveraging its U.S. marketing resources into a bigger share of the domestic market, analysts said on Friday.
The beverage giant reported earnings of $0.31 per share for the fourth quarter and $1.40 for 1996 as a whole. Both figures were right on the respective Wall Street forecasts, according to First Call.

But while earnings were as expected, analysts said the results contained underlying rates of volume growth that exceeded internal performance targets disclosed by Coke executives at a meeting with analysts in December.
"To give you some examples, they said the retail take-away of their products -- what they call case sales -- would grow 10 percent. They were up 11 percent," said Dean Witter analyst David Adelman.
"Their target was that Africa would be up 12-13 percent; It was up 18 percent. They talked about the Greater Europe Group generating 10-11 percent growth. It was up 13 percent."
Overseas business is crucial for Coke because the company derives about 80 percent of its operating profits growth from markets outside the United States.
And even more heartening for overseas prospects than fourth-quarter volume growth was an increasing contribution from emerging markets such as China and Eastern Europe.

Some analysts said China's portion of foreign shipments could be expected to double from two percent in 1995 to four percent in 1998 and climb by a full percentage point per year thereafter. A similar rate of acceleration could be expected for Eastern Europe.

"Both China and India are markets that are going to go like gangbusters, and plus the rest of Asia too. So, what you have is tremendous visibility for Coca-Cola any way you look at it," said PaineWebber's Manny Goldman.
"It's what's necessary for long-term growth and that's important because the stock's priced for long-term growth."

Analysts attributed Coke's overseas success to stronger bottling networks in Europe and Asia, noting specifically the establishment last year of an anchor bottler in Germany and the increased European presence of Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc, in which Coke holds a 45 percent stake.

Domestically, Coke was able to raise its market share from 41 percent to 42 percent partly because of some missteps by arch-rival PepsiCo Inc, analysts said. But they also ascribed the home-front improvement to the growing impact of Coca-Cola's marketing campaigns, including packaging innovations such as the wider use of the contour shape.

As an example of marketing success, analysts pointed to Sprite, which had volumes up 17 percent last year after a 13 percent growth rate in 1995 and an 11 percent improvement the year before that. "That's in the U.S., in a -- quote -- mature market," noted Dean Witter's Adelman.
The Street expects Coke to earn $1.64 per share this year, according to First Call. That would represent an EPS growth rate of more than 17 percent.
Analysts believe the company's annual earnings could advance another 19 percent from there, to reach $1.95 per share in 1998.
Coke's stock was 5/8 higher at 58-1/8 on the New York Stock Exchange in mid-afternoon trading.
